title: When memory fades
hookLine: Emerson at a friend's coffin: the name was gone, the kindness wasn't
tomorrow: why would a dying man remember he owed someone a rooster?

cards: A photo lands in a family group chat: a grandmother in a cardigan, and under it, she didn't know my name today, but she asked if I'd eaten. There's an older version of that text.
The story is told of Ralph Waldo Emerson in his last years, when words had started slipping away from him. Reaching for the word umbrella, he'd come out with the thing that strangers take away.

At the funeral of his old friend, the poet Longfellow, he stood looking at the face in the coffin and said, as the story goes, that this gentleman was a sweet, beautiful soul, but he had entirely forgotten his name.

teach.h: HE COULD STILL SAY WHAT HE WAS.
teach.b: So the name was gone. Look at what wasn't. Emerson couldn't say who his friend was, but he could still say what he was: sweet, beautiful, a soul.
Long before, in an essay called The Over-Soul, Emerson had written about exactly this.

teach.h: THE SOUL IS NOT THE MEMORY.
teach.b: The soul in a person, he said, "is not a function, like the power of memory, of calculation, of comparison, but uses these as hands and feet."
That's a thread through Emerson's Transcendentalism: underneath the mind's tools is a soul, one he believed every person shares in, the Over-Soul.

teach.h: IT USES MEMORY LIKE HANDS AND FEET.
teach.b: Memory is a hand. The soul is the one using it. So when the hand weakens, by Emerson's own teaching, the soul hasn't left.

At the coffin, the tool for names was failing, and the love still worked. That's what this path takes from him: when memory fades, in someone you love or someday in you, don't measure the person by what they can recall.

teach.h: NO QUIZZING: IT'S GOOD TO SEE YOU.
teach.b: Being gentle with memory means no quizzing.
Not, do you know who I am? Just, it's good to see you.

how: People who take this from Emerson greet someone whose memory is fading warmly instead of quizzing them, and look for what still comes through: kindness, humor, care.

o: a way of training your memory to stay sharp
a stage of grief after losing someone you love
when names slip but the person still shows through

games.q: the names go, the soul stays: tap the pairs.
p: forgot the name, kept the kindness
the friend: a sweet, beautiful soul
a tool the soul uses, like hands
the soul Emerson believed all share in

s: at his friend's funeral, Emerson forgot the name but called him a sweet, beautiful soul
as the story is told of Longfellow's funeral: the name was gone, the warmth wasn't.
for Emerson, your soul is basically your memory
he wrote that the soul is not a function like memory; it uses memory as hands and feet.
if someone forgets your name, they've forgotten you
the popular fear. in Emerson's teaching, the soul under the names can still come through.

games.q: your grandfather calls you by your cousin's name all through dinner, happily. what fits Emerson's teaching?
o: answer warmly and enjoy him; the soul is coming through, the label isn't.
correct him gently each time so the right name sticks for next visit.
keep the visit short so the wrong names don't upset him later.
games.why: Emerson wrote that the soul uses memory like hands and feet; it isn't the memory. at Longfellow's coffin the name failed and the love didn't.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose memory is fading, or simply someone older you love. For a few slow breaths, set aside what they've forgotten and name, silently, one kindness of theirs that's still there.
If no one comes to mind, turn it toward yourself: one thing you keep forgetting, met gently.

wordCard.voice: When memory fades: names and facts slip, and in Emerson's teaching the soul that used them doesn't. What comes through is the kindness.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness stays. The name went first, and the sweet, beautiful soul stayed. Day three of seven, done.
